title: Baruch
subtitle: a scribe's book for exiles: confession, wisdom, a mother's comfort, and a letter against idols
lead: Baruch is a short book of the Greek Old Testament set among the Jews taken to Babylon. It opens by saying that Baruch, the scribe of the prophet Jeremiah, wrote it in Babylon in the fifth year after the Chaldeans burned Jerusalem, and read it aloud to King Jeconiah and the exiles (1:1–4). It holds four different pieces: a prose frame in which the exiles send money and a book to Jerusalem (1:1–14); a long confession of the nation's sins, close in wording to Daniel's prayer (1:15–3:8); a poem that asks where wisdom can be found and answers that God gave it to Israel as the Law (3:9–4:4); and a poem in which Jerusalem speaks as a mother to her exiled children and is then told to look east and see them coming home (4:5–5:9).

Chapter 6 is a separate work, the Letter of Jeremiah, written in Jeremiah's name to Jews about to be carried to Babylon. It mocks the gilded gods carried in Babylon's processions, item by item, and ends round after round with a refrain: they are not gods, so have no fear of them. Greek and Orthodox Bibles print it as its own book after Lamentations; the Latin Bible, Catholic Bibles and the King James Version print it as Baruch's sixth chapter. This site follows that numbering but treats the Letter as its own work throughout.

Who reads it as Scripture. The Catholic Church counts Baruch, with the Letter as its chapter 6, among the deuterocanonical books, and the Orthodox churches read Baruch and the Letter as two books of their Old Testament; the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts Baruch too. Anglicans and Lutherans place them among the Apocrypha, books read for example of life but not to establish doctrine; Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches do not count them as Scripture, and they are not in the Jewish Bible. Jeremiah's book page asks the question side by side for each church ("Are Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah part of the Bible?"); this page does not repeat it. Scholars disagree about almost everything else: who wrote the pieces, when, and in what language. The proposals for Baruch run from the 500s BC to after AD 70; for the Letter, from the Persian period to the 100s BC.
facts: The Catholic Church ("Jeremias, with Baruch" in the list of the Council of Trent, 1546; Baruch is in the Catechism's list, 120), the Eastern Orthodox churches (Baruch and the Letter as two books), and the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church (Baruch in the narrower list of its canon, the Letter inside a longer book of Jeremiah's). Among the Apocrypha for Anglicans ("Baruch the Prophet," Article VI) and Lutherans. Not Scripture for Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches, or for Judaism.

Baruch 1–5 names Baruch son of Neriah, Jeremiah's scribe (1:1). Older Catholic scholars defended his authorship, some granting that he compiled earlier pieces. Most critical scholars think two or three unknown Jewish writers composed the parts and an editor joined them, long after Baruch. The Letter's title names Jeremiah (6:1); most scholars, and Jerome, think someone else wrote it in his name.

Baruch: disputed. The book's own date is the fifth year after the fall of Jerusalem, about 582 BC (1:2). Scholars have proposed the Persian period, the 100s BC (Toy), before 100 BC (Harwell) and after AD 70 (Kneucker, Schürer, Whitehouse). Irenaeus quoted it as Jeremiah's words about AD 180. The Letter: a Hebrew original, if there was one, has been dated anywhere from the 500s to the 100s BC; C. J. Ball read its "seven generations" (6:2) as a clue to about 317–306 BC. The Greek of the Letter was made after Alexander's conquests, likely in the 200s or 100s BC (Adams).
Babylon, among the exiles of Jeconiah's deportation, by the river Sud (1:4), with a book and money sent to Jerusalem (1:7–14). The Letter is addressed to Jews about to be led away to Babylon (6:1).
Unknown. Proposals include Judea, Babylonia, Egypt and the wider dispersion; for the Letter, Egypt (Alexandria), Babylon and Palestine have all been suggested (Adams).

Disputed. Many scholars hold that the prose of 1:1–3:8 was translated from Hebrew; the poems are argued both ways; some think the whole book was Greek from the start. For the Letter, most scholars of the 1900s argued for a lost Hebrew original, and some recent scholars read it as Greek composition (Adams).

Greek: Codex Vaticanus (300s AD, the text Swete prints), Alexandrinus (400s), Marchalianus (500s) and Venetus, with later minuscules; Codex Sinaiticus lacks both works. A tiny Greek papyrus from Qumran Cave 7 (7Q2) is thought to hold part of the Letter. Ancient versions: Syriac (including the Syro-Hexapla, made from Origen's Greek in the 600s), Old Latin (taken into the Vulgate), Coptic, Ethiopic, Arabic and Armenian. No Hebrew copy survives of either work.

Baruch: a prose narrative frame, a national confession and prayer, a wisdom poem and a poem of lament and consolation. The Letter: a sermon against idols in the form of a letter, with a repeated refrain.
6 chapters, 213 verses: Baruch 1–5 (141 verses) and the Letter of Jeremiah (chapter 6, 72 verses), in the numbering of Swete's Greek text
authorship: Baruch son of Neriah wrote Baruch 1–5 in Babylon, as 1:1 says, and Jeremiah wrote the Letter. Early Christian writers often quoted Baruch as the words of Jeremiah himself: Irenaeus quotes 4:36–5:9 as what "Jeremiah the prophet has pointed out" (Against Heresies 5.35.1), and Cyprian quotes 3:36–38 under Jeremiah's name (Testimonies 2.6). Francis Gigot's article in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1907) defended Baruch's authorship and allowed that he may have joined several earlier documents; it argued that an inspired editor would leave the book inspired either way.

Critical scholars since the 1800s have generally seen two or three pieces from different hands. The prose of 1:1–3:8 draws whole clauses from Daniel 9 and much from Jeremiah and Deuteronomy; the wisdom poem draws on Job 28, Proverbs 8 and Sirach 24; the last poem draws on Isaiah 40–66 and is very close to Psalms of Solomon 11 (Whitehouse; Toy). An editor, perhaps the writer of the prose, joined them and set them in Baruch's name (Harwell). C. H. Toy wrote in 1902 that "very few scholars" still held that Jeremiah's secretary wrote it.

The Letter is a separate work, as nearly all writers agree, Catholic ones included: it has its own title and its own subject. Jerome called it a pseudepigraph, a writing under a borrowed name, as Gigot reports. C. J. Ball thought its picture of Babylonian worship was firsthand and its author a Jew of the eastern dispersion writing to keep waverers from the temples. Many scholars think its writer built on Jeremiah 10:1–16 and on the real letter of Jeremiah 29 (Adams).

audience.to: Jews living under foreign rule, whether in the dispersion or in a Judea that felt itself still in exile, centuries after the Babylonian captivity. The book is set among the exiles of the 500s BC, but its frame asks for it to be read out "in the Lord's house" on feast days (1:14), so it was written to be heard by a gathered community. Some Jewish groups that read Greek read it in worship: the Apostolic Constitutions (about AD 380) say that Jews read Lamentations and Baruch on the tenth day of the month Gorpiaeus, which C. H. Toy took to be probably the month of Ab, when the fall of the Temple was mourned. The Letter is written to people who live among idol worship and are tempted to fear it (6:4–5).
audience.why: To give exiles words to pray and reasons to hope. The confession teaches them to say that God is just and the shame is theirs (1:15–2:10), and to ask mercy for his name's sake (2:11–3:8). The wisdom poem tells them why they are in a foreign land, because they left the fountain of wisdom (3:10–12), and where life is to be found: in the book of God's commands, which belongs to Israel (4:1–4). The mother's poem gives them Jerusalem's own voice, grieving and then comforted, and promises their return (4:5–5:9). The Letter answers a daily temptation: the splendid gods of a powerful empire, carried shoulder-high through the streets, are wood and metal and cannot save. Knowing the readers changes the reading. Baruch is not a report about Baruch; it is a service book for a people who keep asking why they are still scattered, and the Letter is a sermon for people surrounded by other people's gods.
views: Exiles in Babylon (the book's own setting)

Read as it presents itself, Baruch was sent from Babylon to Jerusalem about 582 BC, and the Letter went to the captives of Jeconiah's deportation. Catholic scholars of the early 1900s, such as Gigot, held this view.
C. H. Toy dated the confession after Daniel and the poems to the early Maccabean period, so that the first readers were Judeans under the Seleucid kings, still waiting for the scattered to come home.
After the Temple's fall in AD 70

Kneucker, Schürer and O. C. Whitehouse read 'Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar his son' (1:11–12) as a mask for Vespasian and his son Titus, and the burning of the Temple (1:2; 2:26) as the burning of AD 70. On this view the first readers were Jews who had to live under Rome after the catastrophe; Whitehouse suggested the circle of Johanan ben Zakkai. Gigot answered that Catholics easily disprove this date, and Harwell argued that Irenaeus's use of it as part of Jeremiah points earlier.

Whatever the date of the Hebrew pieces, the Greek book reached Jews who read the Greek Jeremiah, since its Greek is close to the second half of Greek Jeremiah (Thackeray, as Harwell reports). Ball and Adams think the Letter was read by Jews living among Babylonian or other Gentile worship.

outline: Baruch writes a book in Babylon and reads it to Jeconiah and the exiles; they weep, fast and collect money
The letter to Jerusalem: offer sacrifices, pray for Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar, read this book on the feast days
The confession: justice belongs to the Lord, shame to us; we did not listen
The prayer for mercy: remember your people, as you promised through Moses and the prophets
The wisdom poem: Israel in exile for leaving the fountain of wisdom; no one found her but God, who gave her to Jacob as the book of his commands
Jerusalem speaks as a mother to her exiled children: take courage
Jerusalem comforted: look east, take off your mourning, God is bringing your children home
The Letter of Jeremiah: the title, seven generations in Babylon, gods carried on shoulders, do not fear them
Round after round against the idols: their tongues, their clothes, their priests, their helplessness, each ending in the refrain that they are not gods

lenses.name: Catholic
lenses.desc: The Catholic Church counts Baruch, with the Letter of Jeremiah as its chapter 6, among the deuterocanonical books. The Council of Trent (1546) listed "Jeremias, with Baruch" as sacred and canonical, and the Easter Vigil reads Baruch's wisdom poem (3:9–15, 32–4:4).

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Orthodox churches read Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah as two books after Jeremiah, in the Greek order. Athanasius and Cyril of Jerusalem counted both with Jeremiah among the canonical books, and Orthodox worship reads Baruch under Jeremiah's name on the eve of the Nativity.

lenses.name: Protestant
lenses.desc: Protestants place Baruch and the Letter among the Apocrypha. Anglican and Lutheran Bibles long printed them between the Testaments, to be read for example of life but not to establish doctrine (Article VI names "Baruch the Prophet"); Reformed and Baptist confessions give them no authority.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most critical scholars read Baruch as a collection of pieces by different hands, built from Daniel, Jeremiah, Deuteronomy, Job, Isaiah and the wisdom books and set in Baruch's name, and the Letter as a separate Jewish sermon against idols in Jeremiah's name. Their dates and original languages are debated.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: Neither work is in the Jewish Bible, and Jerome says the Hebrews of his day did not read Baruch. But Greek-speaking Jews read it, perhaps in a day of mourning for the Temple, and rabbinic tradition remembers Baruch in Babylon as Ezra's teacher (Megillah 16b).

sections.b:
Read it as a book of four voices, put in the mouth of a scribe in exile. First the narrator, who sets the scene in Babylon and sends the book to Jerusalem with money and a request: pray for the king, and read this book aloud on the feast days (1:1–14). Then the people, who confess as one: the Lord is in the right, and we are ashamed (1:15–3:8). Then a wisdom teacher, who asks where understanding lives and answers that God found it and gave it to Israel as the book of his commands (3:9–4:4). Last, Jerusalem herself, a widowed mother who sent her children away weeping and is told to put on the robe of glory and watch them come home (4:5–5:9).

The movement is the point. The book goes from the past (why the exile happened) to the present (what to hold on to) to the future (the return). It follows the pattern of Deuteronomy 28–30: sin, curse, exile, turning back to God, and return to the land, which the prayer quotes almost word for word (2:29–35).

Then read chapter 6 as a different piece. The Letter of Jeremiah has its own title, its own audience and its own subject. Its humor is deliberate. Its writer piles up the gods' indignities, from the dust on their faces to the cats on their heads, and closes round after round with nearly the same words, so the hearers say the refrain with him.

The Plain follows the Greek of H. B. Swete's Old Testament in Greek (vol. 3, 1912), which prints Codex Vaticanus and gives the other great codices in its notes. Where the Plain follows another witness, a variant entry says so. The King James Apocrypha, the Latin Vulgate and the Douay-Rheims made from it are used to check sense only. No Hebrew text of either work survives, so every Hebraism or proposed Hebrew original mentioned on these pages is a scholar's reconstruction, labeled as such.

Verse numbers. This site keys every verse to Swete's numbering. The King James Version numbers some verses one lower: its 3:35–37 are this site's 3:36–38, and in chapter 6 the KJV makes the title a verse of its own, so its 6:2–73 are this site's 6:1–72. When you compare a KJV verse with this site, check the words, not only the number. The Orthodox reading "Baruch 3:35–4:4" on the eve of the Nativity is this site's 3:36–4:4.

Names. The Plain uses the forms English Bibles use (Jeconiah, Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Joakim), with the Greek in a note where it differs.

The confession (1:15–3:8). Its first part follows Daniel's prayer (Daniel 9:4–19) so closely that many clauses match, starting with "to us belongs the shame of our faces" (compare Daniel 9:7). C. H. Toy and O. C. Whitehouse thought Baruch borrows from Daniel, because Baruch's version is longer and repeats itself more; Ewald thought the borrowing went the other way. The prayer also weaves in Jeremiah (the yoke of the king of Babylon, Jeremiah 27:11–12; the voice of the bride and groom silenced, Jeremiah 7:34) and Deuteronomy 28–30.

The wisdom poem (3:9–4:4). It asks Job's question, "But wisdom: where can it be found?" (Job 28:12), answers in the language of Proverbs 8 and Deuteronomy 30:12–13, and draws on Sirach 24, where wisdom makes her home in Israel (Whitehouse). It is the clearest place in the book where wisdom and the Law become one (4:1).

The mother's poem (4:5–5:9). Jerusalem's voice comes from Lamentations 1 and Isaiah 49 and 54; the comfort comes from Isaiah 40 and 60. Its last verses run very close to Psalms of Solomon 11, line for line (Whitehouse prints the two side by side). Whitehouse held that Baruch borrowed from the psalm; R. H. Charles, his editor, thought both adapted one older Hebrew psalm; Harwell judged that the shared ideas were common stock since Second Isaiah and settle nothing.

Greek manuscripts place the Letter at the end of Jeremiah's books, after Lamentations, which follows Baruch (Adams). Latin Bibles attached it to Baruch as a sixth chapter; the King James Version and Catholic Bibles follow the Latin. In the Ethiopian Bible it is "the epistle to the captives," counted as chapter 6 of a longer book of Jeremiah's lamentations, which goes on with the story called 4 Baruch (Cowley).

Its model is Jeremiah's real letter to the exiles, "the letter that the prophet Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem" (Jeremiah 29:1), and Jeremiah's satire on idols in Jeremiah 10:1–16: the scarecrow in the cucumber field (6:69) is the picture of Jeremiah 10:5 in the Hebrew text, which the Greek of Jeremiah lacks (Adams). 2 Maccabees knows a tradition that Jeremiah warned the deported "not to let their minds be led astray when they saw images of gold and silver and the finery on them" (2 Maccabees 2:2); whether that is this Letter is debated.

Its picture of Babylon is concrete: gods carried in procession, priests who take the offerings, lamps, the women in the streets (6:43). C. J. Ball thought these details came from real Babylonian worship of the Persian or early Greek period. Its claim of "seven generations" in Babylon (6:2), instead of Jeremiah's seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10), may be the writer's way of speaking to his own time; the Syriac version changes it to seventy years (Ball). Sean Adams notes that a small Greek papyrus from Qumran Cave 7, 7Q2, is thought to hold verses 43–44, though it has only twenty-two letters and the identification is not certain; if it is the Letter, it is the oldest copy of either work.

sections.h: Baruch and the Letter in worship
sections.b:
Catholic. The Easter Vigil, the night before Easter, has the wisdom poem as its sixth reading (3:9–15, 32–4:4).

Orthodox. On the eve of the Nativity the Orthodox read 3:36–4:4 under the heading "Jeremiah (Baruch 3:35–4:4)"; so on the feast of Christ's birth the church hears the verse many Fathers read of the incarnation, "After this she was seen on earth" (3:38). The heading itself shows the old habit of reading Baruch as part of Jeremiah.

Anglican. Article VI lists "Baruch the Prophet" among the books the Church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners."

Jewish. The Apostolic Constitutions (5.20) say that Jews in their day read Lamentations and Baruch when they gathered on the tenth day of Gorpiaeus, and quote "This is our God" (3:36). C. H. Toy thought this was true at most of some Greek-speaking Jewish groups; the rabbis never counted the book (Bava Batra 14b lists the Prophets without it).

• Baruch son of Neriah. Jeremiah's scribe (Jeremiah 36:4; Jeremiah 45:1). In Jeremiah 43:6 he is taken to Egypt with Jeremiah. See the topic Baruch the Scribe.
  • Jeconiah. Jehoiachin, the king of Judah taken to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12–15).
  • Belshazzar. In Baruch, as in Daniel 5, the son of Nebuchadnezzar (1:11). In Babylonian records he is the son of Nabonidus; see the note at Daniel 5:2 for how readers explain "father" and "son."
  • The river Sud (1:4). Otherwise unknown; the Syriac has a different name (Whitehouse).
  • The Everlasting. In the mother's poem God is called by a title, "the Everlasting" (Greek ho aiōnios, 4:10 and often).
  • Wisdom, understanding, insight. The wisdom poem uses three Greek words, sophia, epistēmē and phronēsis, rendered the same way through the book.
  • The refrain. The Letter closes many rounds with a refrain: "This makes it plain that they are not gods. So have no fear of them" (6:14), with small changes each time.

spec.title: Claude's theory: Baruch's frame is modeled on his brother's scroll
spec.body: Jeremiah 51:59–64 tells how Seraiah son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah, went to Babylon with Zedekiah, carrying a scroll Jeremiah had written. He was told: "When you reach Babylon, take a look, and read all these words out loud" (Jeremiah 51:61), and then to tie a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates. Jeremiah 32:12 gives Baruch the same father and grandfather, so Seraiah was Baruch's brother. Baruch 1:1–4 tells a matching story: Baruch son of Neriah writes a book in Babylon and reads it aloud to the exiles by a river. The writer may have built his frame on that model, giving the scribe who never went to Babylon in Jeremiah's book the journey his brother made. This would explain why the frame insists on a public reading and names a river. This is my own suggestion; I did not find it in the sources I read, though commentators may have made it.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a service for a day of mourning
spec.body: The frame asks for the book to be read aloud in the Lord's house on feast days (1:14). The Apostolic Constitutions say Jews read Lamentations and Baruch together on a day in the late summer, which C. H. Toy took to be in the month of Ab, when Jews mourned the Temple's fall. The order of the book fits such a day: confession of the sins that brought the disaster (1:15–3:8), a reminder that the Law is still Israel's treasure (3:9–4:4), and comfort drawn from Isaiah 40 and 60 (4:5–5:9). The later synagogue moves the same way, from mourning in Ab to Isaiah's words of comfort. If the book was used like this, its four pieces may have been gathered for one service, which would explain why such different writings were joined. This is my own theory, built on the two pieces of evidence above; Toy doubted the reading was ever widespread.

prompts: Baruch reads the book by the river (1:3–4)

A scribe in a plain robe stands on a low rise by a slow river lined with willows, holding open a long scroll and reading aloud; around him sit and stand exiled men and women, a young king in a simple cloak among them, some weeping with their hands over their faces; behind them the brick towers of a great city fade into haze. Style: sketched by hand onto an old scroll, ink and faded earth colors, mixing ancient manuscript drawing with cave-painting figures and loose modern lines; soft torn edges, no hard border or rectangle.

A tall woman with a city wall and towers drawn as a crown on her head stands on a hilltop; on one side of her, in gray, she wears sackcloth and waves farewell to a line of children led away by soldiers; on the other side, in warm gold, she wears a shining robe and a high headdress and looks east, where the same children come back over leveled hills, carried high as if on thrones, under trees that lean over them for shade. Style: hand-drawn on an aged scroll, ink wash and gold leaf, part medieval manuscript, part cave drawing, part modern sketch; soft edges, no frame.

A street procession in ancient Babylon: priests carry wooden gods covered in gold and silver on their shoulders; the gods' faces are blackened with lamp smoke, a bat clings to one head, swallows circle another, and a cat sits on a shoulder; at the side of the street a small group of exiles watches, unafraid, one of them pointing and smiling. Style: sketched onto a scroll with brown ink and faded color, mixing Babylonian relief carving, cave-drawing figures and modern cartoon lines; soft edges, no hard rectangle.
The scarecrow in the cucumber field (6:69)

A small field of cucumber vines under a pale sky; in the middle a scarecrow made of a post and rags, painted with a gold face like a temple statue; crows sit unbothered on its arms and pick at the vines. Style: quick hand sketch on an old scroll, ink and watercolor, half ancient manuscript, half modern drawing; soft torn edges, no border.
reading: Sean A. Adams, Baruch and the Epistle of Jeremiah: A Commentary Based on the Texts in Codex Vaticanus (Brill, 2014)
A recent commentary on the Greek of both works, from the same manuscript this site translates; it reads the Greek largely without a presumed Hebrew original.
Carey A. Moore, Daniel, Esther and Jeremiah: The Additions (Anchor Bible 44, 1977)
A standard English commentary on Baruch and the Letter with the other additions.
O. C. Whitehouse, "I Baruch," and C. J. Ball, "Epistle of Jeremy," in R. H. Charles, ed., The Apocrypha and Pseudepigrapha of the Old Testament, vol. 1 (1913)
Old but thorough introductions and notes, now public domain; Whitehouse argues for a date after AD 70, Ball for a Hebrew Letter of about 300 BC.
Robert R. Harwell, The Principal Versions of Baruch (1915)
A short public-domain study of the Greek, Syriac and Latin, with the case for a Hebrew original and a date before 100 BC.
Joseph Ziegler, ed., Jeremias, Baruch, Threni, Epistula Jeremiae (Göttingen Septuagint 15)
The critical edition of the Greek, with every manuscript reading; for advanced study.

canon.summary: Baruch, with the Letter of Jeremiah as its chapter 6, is in the Old Testament of the Catholic Church; the Orthodox churches read Baruch and the Letter as two books, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts Baruch too. Anglicans and Lutherans place them among the Apocrypha, read for example of life but not to establish doctrine; Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches do not count them as Scripture, and they are not in the Jewish Bible.
accepted_by: Scripture, one of the deuterocanonical books, with the Letter of Jeremiah as its sixth chapter. The Council of Trent (Session 4, 8 April 1546) listed "Jeremias, with Baruch" among the sacred and canonical books, and declared anathema anyone who does not receive these books "entire with all their parts" as they are in the old Latin Vulgate. The Catechism (120) names Baruch between Lamentations and Ezekiel. Jerome had left Baruch out of his translation from the Hebrew (see below); the Latin Baruch of the Vulgate is the older Latin version, later added to it (Whitehouse).

In the Old Testament, as two books after Jeremiah in the Greek order, Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah, and read in worship under Jeremiah's name: the readings for the eve of the Nativity include "Jeremiah (Baruch 3:35–4:4)." Baruch has a stronger place than most of the books outside the Hebrew Bible, because the old Greek lists counted it with Jeremiah inside the 22 books: Athanasius (367) has "Jeremiah with Baruch, Lamentations, and the epistle, one book," Cyril of Jerusalem (about 350) has the same, and so does canon 60 of Laodicea, whose genuineness is doubted. The Orthodox Church in America's answer counts "the Prophecy of Baruch" among the books "accepted by Orthodox Christianity as canonical scripture." The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named other books of the Greek Bible but not these two, and Philaret's catechism (1839) lists only "of Jeremiah" among the 22.

Scripture. Cowley's study of the canon lists Baruch among the books of the narrower count of the 81-book Bible. In the Ethiopic Bible Jeremiah 1–52 is followed by Baruch (five chapters, shorter than the Greek) and by a book of Jeremiah's lamentations that holds Lamentations 1–5, "the epistle to the captives" (the Letter) as its chapter 6, and the story known as 4 Baruch.
Other Oriental Orthodox churches (Coptic, Syriac, Armenian)

Read in their own ancient translations, all made from the Greek: Syriac (including the Syro-Hexapla of 616–617), Coptic in both Bohairic and Sahidic (the Sahidic including the Letter), and Armenian (Whitehouse). Ephrem the Syrian (300s) treated Baruch as Scripture (Whitehouse).

Among the Apocrypha. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles names "Baruch the Prophet" among the other books which, "as Hierome saith," the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not apply "to establish any doctrine." The Letter is not named separately; the King James Version (1611), made in the same church, prints it as Baruch's sixth chapter.
Among the Apocrypha. Luther's complete German Bible (1534) printed Baruch, with the Letter of Jeremiah, among the Apocrypha, books it called not held equal to Holy Scripture.
Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession (1646, 1.3) says the books "commonly called Apocrypha" are not divinely inspired, are no part of the canon, and are of no authority in the church.
Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) repeats Westminster almost word for word. Most evangelical churches hold the 66 books.

Not Scripture. The Talmud's order of the Prophets (Bava Batra 14b) has no Baruch, and Jerome says the Hebrews of his day neither read nor had it. Some Greek-speaking Jews did read it: the Apostolic Constitutions (about 380) say that Jews read Lamentations and Baruch on the tenth of Gorpiaeus. Rabbinic tradition remembers Baruch himself as Ezra's teacher in Babylonia (Megillah 16b).

Widely used, usually as part of Jeremiah. Irenaeus (about 180) quotes 4:36–5:9 as the words of "Jeremiah the prophet," Cyprian quotes 3:36–38 under Jeremiah's name, and Hippolytus answers the followers of Noetus, who used the same verses (Whitehouse adds Athenagoras, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Tertullian and Lactantius). Origen's list, as Eusebius gives it, has "Jeremiah, with Lamentations and the epistle in one," and does not name Baruch. Jerome alone set Baruch aside, because it was not in the Hebrew.

provenance.h: When and where it was written
provenance.b:
The book gives its own date: the fifth year, on the seventh of a month it does not name, "the time when the Chaldeans captured Jerusalem and set it on fire" (1:2), so about 582 BC. Whitehouse noted that some (Fritzsche, Gifford) counted from the fall of 587–586 BC and others (Eichhorn, Kneucker) from the first capture of 597, when the Temple still stood, which would better fit the offerings of 1:10.

Scholars who do not take the frame at face value have offered every period after that. Ewald put the prose at the end of the Persian empire. C. H. Toy (1902) thought the confession came after Daniel and the poems belong to the early Maccabean period. Harwell (1915) argued that the whole book was translated into Greek before the Christian era, by the hand that translated the second half of Greek Jeremiah, and that the poems may be older than the Maccabees. Kneucker, Schürer and Whitehouse (1913) read it after AD 70, with Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar standing for Vespasian and Titus; Whitehouse put the prose about AD 74 and the mother's poem a few years later. Gigot's Catholic Encyclopedia article answered that Catholics "easily disprove" so late a date. The latest possible date is fixed by Irenaeus, who quotes the book about AD 180.

For the Letter, Ball (1913) argued from its "seven generations" (6:2) that it was written about 317–306 BC, among Babylonian Jews; Adams (2020) says that a Hebrew original, if it existed, was written between the 500s and 100s BC, and that the Greek came after Alexander, likely in the 200s or 100s BC. The place is unknown for both works.

No Hebrew text of either work survives, and the evidence is indirect.

  • Hebraisms. The Greek of 1:1–3:8 reads like translation: Whitehouse lists words such as manna for the grain offering (1:10) and Hebrew-style relative clauses (2:4; 2:26), and by 1913 nearly all scholars agreed the prose was translated from Hebrew. The wisdom poem was argued both ways; Whitehouse thought the mother's poem was Greek from the start, while his editor R. H. Charles found a Hebraism in 5:6 and argued for Hebrew. Harwell (1915) argued for Hebrew throughout.
  • Origen's marks. The Syro-Hexapla, a Syriac translation of Origen's Greek made in 616–617, has a note at the end saying the whole book was under the obelus, Origen's sign for what is not in the Hebrew. Yet in the margin at 1:17 and 2:3 it notes three times "not found in the Hebrew," and it marks one clause in 2:1 with an asterisk. Whitehouse and Gigot took these notes as evidence of a Hebrew text; Nestle and Harwell argued that they refer to the passages Baruch borrows (Daniel 9:8 and the curse of eating one's children), not to a Hebrew Baruch.
  • Theodotion. The Syro-Hexapla's margin gives five readings marked as Theodotion's (Harwell). Gigot thought it "highly probable" that Theodotion translated Baruch from Hebrew; Harwell thought Theodotion revised the Greek.
  • Jerome says only that the Hebrews neither read nor have the book.
  • The Letter. Ball and most scholars of the 1900s argued for a Hebrew original, explaining odd Greek phrases as misread Hebrew ("marble" and "linen" in 6:71 are one example). Fritzsche and Schürer in the 1800s, and Benjamin Wright and Sean Adams more recently, read it as Greek composition (Adams).

The Greek is in Codex Vaticanus (300s AD), which Swete prints and this site translates, in Alexandrinus (400s), Marchalianus (500s) and Venetus, and in later minuscules; Sinaiticus does not have either work, probably because of a gap in the manuscript after Lamentations 2:20 (Adams). For the Letter, Adams judges Vaticanus the best text, with few and minor differences among the codices. A papyrus fragment from Qumran Cave 7, 7Q2, all of whose legible fragments are Greek (VanderKam), is thought to hold Letter 43–44 in a form close to the later Lucianic Greek, but has only twenty-two letters (Adams). Nothing of Baruch 1–5 has been found at Qumran (VanderKam).

The ancient translations were all made from the Greek: Syriac (an ordinary version and the Syro-Hexapla), two Old Latin versions (one of which became the Vulgate's Baruch), Arabic, Ethiopic, Coptic and Armenian (Whitehouse; Harwell). Jerome did not translate either work, and the oldest Vulgate manuscript, Codex Amiatinus, does not have them (Whitehouse).

provenance.h: What it builds on in the Hebrew Bible
provenance.b:
Both works are made largely of earlier Scripture, and the links run from the Hebrew Bible to Baruch.

  • Daniel 9:4–19: whole clauses of the confession (1:15–2:19).
  • Jeremiah: the call to serve the king of Babylon (2:21–23; Jeremiah 27:11–12), the silenced voices of joy (2:23; Jeremiah 7:34), the everlasting covenant (2:35; Jeremiah 32:40); the Letter builds on Jeremiah 10:1–16 and Jeremiah 29.
  • Deuteronomy 28–32: the curses, eating one's children (2:3), the nation from far away (4:15), the return (2:29–35), and the sacrifice "to demons, not to God" (4:7; Deuteronomy 32:17).
  • Job 28, Proverbs 8 and Deuteronomy 30:12–13: the search for wisdom (3:15–31).
  • Isaiah 40–66: the comfort of Jerusalem, the leveled hills and the children carried home (4:36–5:9; Isaiah 40:4; Isaiah 60:4).
  • Psalm 115 and Isaiah 44:9–20: idols that cannot see, speak or save (chapter 6).

It also has close links outside the Hebrew Bible: Sirach 24 in the wisdom poem, Psalms of Solomon 11 in the last verses, and 2 Maccabees 2:1–3 with the Letter.

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: The Jewish Bible's Prophets are Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Kings, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Isaiah and the Twelve (Bava Batra 14b); Baruch is not among them, and no Hebrew copy of it or of the Letter survives. Protestants and many others hold that the Old Testament the church should receive is the one the Jews kept, "the oracles of God" entrusted to them (Romans 3:2), and that books outside it may be useful but not authoritative.

Jerome, in the preface to his translation of Jeremiah from the Hebrew, wrote that he had left out the book of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, which the Hebrews neither read nor have, and that he expected curses from the jealous for it. He also called the Letter a pseudepigraph, a writing under a false name (as Gigot reports). His Latin Bible had neither work; the Vulgate's Baruch is the Old Latin, added later (Whitehouse). Article VI cites him ("as Hierome saith") for its rule that these books are read for example of life, not to establish doctrine.

Origen's list of the 22 books of the Jews, as Eusebius reports it, has "Jeremiah, with Lamentations and the epistle in one," and leaves Baruch out, though Origen quoted Baruch elsewhere (Whitehouse). The note at the end of the Syro-Hexapla that the whole book was under the obelus (Harwell) means that Origen found no Hebrew text to set beside it.

The Reformers' general case against the Apocrypha applies here: these books are not in the Hebrew canon, the New Testament never quotes them as Scripture, and the church may not make doctrine from them (Westminster Confession 1.3; Article VI). Anglicans and Lutherans kept Baruch for reading. Against Baruch in particular, Protestant writers have pointed to the historical problems of the frame and to the borrowed character of the prose.

Scholars of every church note points in 1:1–14 that are hard to fit with the history in Kings and Jeremiah:

  • Baruch in Babylon. Jeremiah's book last shows Baruch taken to Egypt: "They also took Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch son of Neriah" (Jeremiah 43:6), and they went as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:7). Nothing in the Bible takes him to Babylon. Whitehouse noted that this silence proves little.
  • Belshazzar as Nebuchadnezzar's son (1:11–12), as in Daniel 5, though Babylonian records make him the son of Nabonidus.
  • Sacrifice in a burned Temple. The exiles send money for burnt offerings and incense on the altar (1:10) after the city and house were burned (1:2).
  • Joakim son of Hilkiah, son of Shallum (1:7). The Greek calls him "the priest" (the KJV says "the high priest"). The priestly line in 1 Chronicles 6:13–15 runs Shallum, Hilkiah, Azariah, Seraiah, Jehozadak, and the head priest in 586 BC was Seraiah (2 Kings 25:18); a high priest Joiakim appears only after the return (Nehemiah 12:10, 26).
  • The vessels (1:8): silver vessels said to have been made by Zedekiah and sent back, which the history books do not mention.
  • The Letter's "seven generations" (6:2) instead of Jeremiah's seventy years (Jeremiah 29:10).

rejected_why.h: How the churches that keep it answer
rejected_why.b:
On the canon. Those who keep the books point out that the church read Baruch as part of Jeremiah from the 100s on (Irenaeus, Cyprian, Hippolytus), and that the Greek lists of Athanasius, Cyril and Laodicea counted Baruch and the Letter inside the canon even when they set other books outside it. Trent defined the list the Western church had long read.

On Baruch in Babylon. Whitehouse noted that Jeremiah's book says nothing of Baruch after Egypt, so a later journey cannot be ruled out, and a rabbinic tradition places Baruch in Babylonia, where Ezra stayed with him as his disciple until Baruch died (Megillah 16b).

On the dates and names. For "father" and "son," defenders of Daniel give the same answers here (see the note at Daniel 5:2). For the offerings, Jeremiah 41:5 shows men bringing "grain offerings and frankincense" to the house of the LORD after the Temple was burned, so some worship went on at the site (Whitehouse); counting the fifth year from 597, when the Temple still stood, also removes the problem. Gigot wrote that Catholic answers are considered sufficient by Catholic scholars generally.

On the kind of book. Catholic teaching since the Second Vatican Council says that truth "is set forth and expressed differently in texts which are variously historical, prophetic, poetic" and so on, and that Scripture teaches "that truth which God wanted put into sacred writings for the sake of salvation" (Dei Verbum 11–12). On this teaching a Catholic reader may take the frame of Baruch and the title of the Letter as a literary setting rather than a historical report without denying that the books are inspired. Gigot argued in 1907 that if an inspired editor joined the parts, the book remains inspired.

cited_in.b: Paul applies Deuteronomy 30:12–14 to Christ: "Who will go up into heaven?" (Romans 10:6). Baruch applies the same verses to wisdom: who climbed up into the sky and took her, who crossed to the far side of the sea and found her (3:29–30). Both reuse Deuteronomy for something God gives that no one could fetch. Paul's "abyss" (Romans 10:7) is in neither Deuteronomy nor Baruch, and his words follow Deuteronomy, not Baruch, so there is no sign that he used Baruch; the link is a shared way of reading Deuteronomy 30.

"The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14). Many Fathers read 3:38 as a prophecy of this: "After this she was seen on earth" (3:38). The Greek verb has no stated subject; the Plain takes it as wisdom, while the KJV, the Syriac (Whitehouse) and Cyprian read "he," meaning God. Cyprian cites 3:36–38 to prove that Christ is God, and Hippolytus and Origen used it too. There is no shared wording in the Greek (John's eskēnōsen, Baruch's synanestraphē); John's "pitched his tent" is closer to Sirach 24:8, where wisdom pitches her tent in Jacob. Many critics (Toy; the scholars Whitehouse lists) think 3:38 is a later Christian addition; others read it as wisdom living in Israel through the Law (4:1). So the link is the Fathers' reading, not a quotation.

"What they sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20). Baruch's "offering sacrifices to demons and not to God" (4:7) and Paul's share the same words, but both come from Deuteronomy 32:17, "They offered sacrifices to demons, not to God," in its Greek form, which Baruch follows closely (Whitehouse). A shared source, not a quotation of Baruch.

Survivors who would not give up "idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone, and wood, which are not able to see or hear or walk" (Revelation 9:20). The Letter mocks "silver gods, gold gods and wooden gods" (6:3) that cannot see, help or save. Revelation's list of metals and of what idols cannot do is closer to Daniel 5:23 and Psalm 115:4–7, so this is the common Jewish satire on idols, not a use of the Letter.

"Many will come from the sunrise and the sunset" (Matthew 8:11). Baruch pictures Jerusalem's children gathered from east and west (4:37; 5:5). Both draw on Isaiah's promise of a gathering from the sunrise and the sunset (Isaiah 43:5); there is no sign of direct dependence.

Jesus says "nobody has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven" (John 3:13). Baruch asks who went up into heaven to bring wisdom down (3:29), as Proverbs 30:4 asks who climbed up to heaven and came back down. A shared biblical question; Christian readers have answered it with Christ, but John does not cite Baruch.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Jewish prayer and hope in the centuries around Jesus, Baruch is valuable: it shows how Jews confessed the nation's sins in the words of Daniel and Deuteronomy, joined wisdom to the Law, and gave Jerusalem a mother's voice; the Letter shows how Jews mocked the gods of their neighbors. Its date is unknown, which limits what it can prove about any one time. As a text, the Greek is well preserved in the great codices, but no Hebrew survives, and the oldest physical trace is a scrap of twenty-two letters that may be the Letter. As history, the frame's details do not fit the history of Kings and Jeremiah, and most scholars read Baruch's name and Jeremiah's as literary settings; the churches that hold the books inspired answer that this is a question of literary form, not of truth. Measured by the 66 books, Baruch mostly repeats and applies them; it goes beyond them in identifying wisdom with the Law and in its picture of Jerusalem's return, and it does not conflict with them in doctrine.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish faith before and around Jesus: high
sections.b: Even on the latest proposed date, Baruch shows a Judaism that prays in the words of Scripture and answers disaster with confession: "Righteousness belongs to the Lord our God, but to us belongs the shame of our faces" (1:15; compare Daniel 9:7). It shows the joining of wisdom and Torah (4:1) also found in Sirach 24, and the hope for a gathering of all Israel from east and west (4:37; 5:5) also found in the Psalms of Solomon. The Letter shows how a Jewish preacher answered the pull of a great empire's worship with satire and a simple rule: do not fear them. The evidence of Greek-speaking Jews reading Baruch with Lamentations (Apostolic Constitutions 5.20) suggests it served in worship. Its value is limited by its uncertain date: it cannot be used to show what Jews believed in one century rather than another.

The Greek of both works is in the great codices from the 300s on, and Adams finds few and minor differences among them for the Letter. Swete's apparatus and the versions show more variation in Baruch 1–5. No Hebrew text survives of either work, so every claim about an original Hebrew is reconstruction, and the Syro-Hexapla's notes "not found in the Hebrew" may refer to the passages Baruch borrows rather than to a Hebrew Baruch (Harwell). The Qumran fragment 7Q2, if it is the Letter, shows that the Greek Letter was being copied before the Christian era; nothing of Baruch 1–5 was found at Qumran (VanderKam). The Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Arabic and Armenian translations were all made from the Greek.

Baruch presents itself as written by Baruch in Babylon about 582 BC; the Letter, as a letter of Jeremiah to the captives. The evidence makes both claims hard to hold as history: Jeremiah 43:6 last shows Baruch in Egypt; Belshazzar is called Nebuchadnezzar's son (1:11), as in Daniel; offerings are sent to a burned Temple (1:2; 1:10); the priest Joakim (1:7) is not in the priestly lists; the confession borrows from Daniel, which most scholars date later; and the Letter's "seven generations" (6:2) do not match Jeremiah's seventy years. There are answers: Baruch's later life is unknown, and rabbinic tradition puts him in Babylon (Megillah 16b); "son" can mean successor; worship went on at the Temple's site (Jeremiah 41:5); the fifth year may be counted from 597. Taken together, the critical case is strong, and most critical scholars read the frame as a setting. The Catholic Church teaches that the truth of a book is to be read according to its literary form (Dei Verbum 12), so this does not settle whether it is inspired. The Letter's details about Babylonian worship, by contrast, look firsthand to Ball.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: God's justice in punishing Israel's sin (1:15–2:10; Daniel 9:7; Deuteronomy 28); his mercy for his own sake and his name's (2:14; 3:5; Daniel 9:18–19); the promise of return after repentance (2:29–35; Deuteronomy 30:1–5; Jeremiah 32:37–41); wisdom as God's gift that no human can fetch (3:15–31; Job 28:12–28); Jerusalem as a bereaved mother comforted by God (4:5–5:9; Lamentations 1; Isaiah 54; Isaiah 60); idols as helpless wood and metal (chapter 6; Psalm 115:4–8; Isaiah 44:9–20; Jeremiah 10:1–16); praying for the rulers of the land of exile (1:11; Jeremiah 29:7).
  • Goes beyond: (a) wisdom is the Law: "the book of the commands of God" (4:1), said more plainly than in Proverbs, close to Sirach 24; (b) 3:38, which Christian readers take as a prophecy of the incarnation (John 1:14), while others read it of wisdom in the Law or as a later addition; (c) demons as the receivers of pagan sacrifice and the dwellers of ruined cities (4:7, 35), as in Deuteronomy 32:17 and Isaiah 13:21, but more developed; (d) seven generations of exile (6:2), a different count from Jeremiah 29:10.
  • Differs or may conflict: no point of doctrine is in conflict with the 66 books. The historical frame differs from Jeremiah 43 (Baruch in Egypt), and the seven generations differ from the seventy years. Protestant readers take these as signs that the books are not Scripture; Catholic and Orthodox readers take them as questions of literary form or of counting.

how_to_read.b: Remember who counts it as Scripture. If you are Catholic or Orthodox, Baruch and the Letter are in your Bible, and your church's teaching and worship are your guide to them. If you are Protestant, they are not Scripture for you, though Anglican and Lutheran tradition commends them for example of life. For each church's answer side by side, see Jeremiah's book page, "Are Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah part of the Bible?"

how_to_read.h: Read it as four pieces and a letter
how_to_read.b: Read the frame (1:1–14), the confession (1:15–3:8), the wisdom poem (3:9–4:4) and the mother's poem (4:5–5:9) one at a time, and ask who is speaking and to whom. Then read chapter 6 as its own work. The chapter pages give each piece its own card on who it was for.

Read Daniel 9:4–19 next to 1:15–2:19, Deuteronomy 28–30 next to 2:20–35, Job 28 and Deuteronomy 30:11–14 next to 3:9–4:4, Lamentations 1 and Isaiah 40, 54 and 60 next to 4:5–5:9, and Jeremiah 10:1–16 and Jeremiah 29 next to chapter 6. You will see how much of the book is Scripture rearranged, and where it adds its own voice.

On the frame's history, on 3:38 and on the Letter's seven generations, the churches and scholars give real answers, set out above and on the chapter pages. Read each in its strongest form before deciding.

how_to_read.h: Using it in study or teaching
how_to_read.b: When you quote it, say what it is: "Baruch, in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Christians and among the Apocrypha for Protestants." Say which numbering you use, since the King James Version numbers some verses one lower (see "About this translation"). It is a good background for how Jews prayed in exile, for wisdom and Law in the New Testament, and for Paul's and Revelation's words about idols.
